lead: A levelling survey finds heights by measuring vertical distances from one fixed zero surface. Three words keep the measurements consistent: datum is that zero surface, benchmark is a point whose height above it is already known, and reduced level is the height of any point above the datum. The level instrument gives a horizontal line of sight; staff readings turn that line into height differences. Road gradients, drainage slopes, canal beds, building plinth levels and contour maps all depend on this chain of heights.
prereq: You need: datums and coordinate systems for MSL, geoid and ellipsoid, and maps and scales for map height notation.

blocks.text: A level surface is a surface on which every point has the same gravitational potential; still water in a pond traces part of one. Mean sea level (MSL) is the average sea surface over a long period, used as the national height zero. A level line is a line that lies on a level surface; it curves with the earth. A horizontal line is straight and tangent to the level line at the instrument; a vertical line is along gravity, at right angles to the level surface. The level instrument sights a horizontal line, not a level line.

The datum is the surface to which all heights are referred. In Indian levelling the datum is normally MSL, and the Survey of India maintains the national height network. Heights above the datum are positive; below it they are negative. A datum is chosen once and quoted with every height, because a height without its datum is meaningless. On a small site an arbitrary datum may be a floor level, but then no height can be compared with a map height.

A benchmark (BM) is a fixed point whose reduced level is known from an earlier survey. A reduced level (RL) is the height of a point above the datum; some syllabi call it the elevation of the point. The RL is written with its datum, for example RL 50.00 m above MSL.

items: GTS benchmark: a mark fixed by the Great Trigonometrical Survey, now maintained through the Survey of India; its RL is published for general use.
Permanent benchmark: a stable brass plate or mark on a building, bridge or plinth, with an RL fixed by a previous survey.
Temporary benchmark: a local stable object, such as a rock or kerb, whose RL is found from a permanent benchmark for one job.
Arbitrary benchmark: a point with an assumed RL, such as 100.000 m, used when no national benchmark is nearby; all heights are then relative.

blocks.text: A station is the place where the instrument is set up. A staff station is the point where the staff is held. The instrument must be protected at a station; a staff station can be any point whose height is wanted.

A backsight (BS) is the first staff reading after the instrument is set up, taken on a point of known RL. A foresight (FS) is the last reading before the instrument is moved, taken on a point whose RL is wanted. An intermediate sight (IS) is any other reading from the same setup. A change point is a staff station read as an FS from one setup and as a BS from the next; it carries the RL forward.

blocks.where: RL(new) is the height of the new point above the datum in m; RL(known) is the height of the known point above the same datum in m; BS is the backsight on the known point in m; FS is the foresight on the new point in m.

blocks.text: The height of instrument (HI) is the RL of the horizontal line of sight: HI = RL + BS. For any point seen from that setup, RL = HI − staff reading. The HI is a reduced level in metres, not the height of the tripod above the ground.

A positive BS − FS means the new point is higher than the known point; a negative value means it is lower. Every change point becomes the known point for the next step, so errors travel forward. Booking and reduction are covered in booking and reduction of levels.

figure.caption: The chain starts at mean sea level, fixes the benchmark, adds the backsight to get the height of instrument, and subtracts the foresight to get the reduced level of point A. Notice that the instrument height is a reduced level, not a distance above the ground.

spec.title: One step of the height chain
spec.aria: A downward chain from mean sea level to a benchmark of known reduced level, then to the height of instrument by adding the backsight, and finally to the reduced level of point A by subtracting the foresight.

examples.question: A benchmark BM has RL 50.00 m. A level is set between BM and point A. The staff on BM reads 2.50 m; the staff on A reads 1.80 m. Find the height of instrument and the reduced level of A. Check the result by the rise-and-fall method.
steps: Given: RL of BM = 50.00 m, BS on BM = 2.50 m, FS on A = 1.80 m.
Height of instrument: HI = RL of BM + BS = 50.00 + 2.50 = 52.50 m.
Check by rise and fall: rise = BS − FS = 2.50 − 1.80 = 0.70 m. A positive rise puts A above BM.
RL(A) = 50.00 + 0.70 = 50.70 m. The two routes agree.
examples.answer: Height of instrument = 52.50 m; reduced level of A = 50.70 m above the same datum.
examples.check:
rl_bm = 50.00
bs = 2.50
fs = 1.80
hi = rl_bm + bs
rl_a = hi - fs
rise = bs - fs
print(hi)
print(rl_a)
print(rise)

traps: Level line and horizontal line are not the same. The level line is curved; the horizontal line is straight and tangent. The instrument sights the horizontal line, so long sights need curvature correction (see curvature and refraction).
Not every staff station is a benchmark. A benchmark has an RL fixed by a previous survey; a staff station gets its RL from the present chain.
HI is the RL of the line of sight, not the height of the tripod. Adding BS to RL gives HI; subtracting a staff reading from HI gives RL.
Sign slip: use RL(new) = RL(known) + BS − FS. If FS is larger than BS, the new point is lower and the RL must fall.
Mixing datums: an arbitrary datum and MSL cannot be mixed in one table without conversion. A height without its datum is not an RL.

quiz.a: Datum: zero surface to which heights are referred. Benchmark: fixed point of known RL.

quiz.q: Why can an RL be negative?
quiz.a: RL is height above datum; a point below datum has negative RL.

quiz.q: Give one difference between BS and IS.
quiz.a: BS is taken on a point of known RL at the start of a setup; IS is any other reading from that setup on a point whose RL is wanted.

quiz.q: A BM has RL 100.000 m. BS = 1.450 m; FS = 2.120 m. Find the RL of the new point.
With HI = 52.50 m, a staff reading on point B is 1.30 m. Find RL of B.
A student writes FS = 18.0 m instead of 1.80 m. What happens to the computed RL of that point?
quiz.a: FS is too large by 16.2 m, so RL = HI − FS is too low by 16.2 m. Any later point using that change point also shifts.

quiz.q: Why is a change point more critical than an ordinary intermediate sight?
quiz.a: The change point becomes the BS for the next setup. An error there passes into every later RL; an IS error affects only that one point.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern total stations store point IDs and compute RL automatically, but the datum and benchmark logic is unchanged. GNSS gives ellipsoidal height; converting to MSL needs a geoid model. Digital level runs and LiDAR point clouds still reduce to height differences. Search next: vertical datum, geoid model, height modernization, digital levelling.
